items.wrong: By the time we got there, the movie already started.
accept: By the time we got there, the movie had already started.
items.hint: Which happened first: getting there, or the movie starting? Use had + the verb for the earlier action.
items.why: When one past action happened before another past action, the earlier one uses the past perfect: had + verb (had started).

items.wrong: I have went to that museum twice.
accept: I have gone to that museum twice.
items.hint: After have, use the past participle. Went or gone?
items.why: Have goes with the past participle: have gone, not have went.

items.wrong: Yesterday Maya walks to the park and played soccer.
accept: Yesterday Maya walked to the park and played soccer.
items.hint: The word yesterday tells you when. Do both verbs match it?
items.why: Both actions happened yesterday, so both verbs should be past tense: walked and played.

items.wrong: Every morning he wakes up early and ate breakfast.
accept: Every morning he wakes up early and eats breakfast.
items.hint: Every morning means it happens again and again. Which tense fits both verbs?
items.why: Something that happens every morning uses present tense for both verbs: wakes and eats.

items.prompt: Fix the pair of joining words.
items.wrong: Neither the cat or the dog wanted to go outside.
accept: Neither the cat nor the dog wanted to go outside.
items.hint: Some joining words come in pairs: either goes with or. What goes with neither?
items.why: Neither pairs with nor, and either pairs with or.

items.prompt: Fix the pair of joining words.
items.wrong: You can either have pizza nor tacos for dinner.
accept: You can either have pizza or tacos for dinner.
You can have either pizza or tacos for dinner.
items.hint: Either goes with which word?
items.why: Either pairs with or (either pizza or tacos).

items.wrong: We packed apples grapes and crackers for the trip.
accept: We packed apples, grapes, and crackers for the trip.
We packed apples, grapes and crackers for the trip.
items.hint: When you list three or more things, put a comma after each item before and.
items.why: Commas separate items in a list of three or more: apples, grapes, and crackers.

items.wrong: After the game ended we went out for ice cream.
accept: After the game ended, we went out for ice cream.
items.hint: The sentence starts with an introduction before the main part. Where does the introduction end?
items.why: Put a comma after an introductory part of a sentence: After the game ended, we went…

items.wrong: Yes Sam I finished my homework.
accept: Yes, Sam, I finished my homework.
items.hint: Use commas to set off yes/no and the name of the person you are talking to.
items.why: Set off yes or no with a comma, and set off the name of the person you're talking to (direct address): Yes, Sam, I…

items.wrong: It's cold today isn't it?
accept: It's cold today, isn't it?
items.hint: A short question tacked on at the end needs a comma before it.
items.why: A tag question at the end of a sentence (isn't it?) is separated with a comma.

items.wrong: Me and Jordan built the volcano together.
accept: Jordan and I built the volcano together.
I and Jordan built the volcano together.
items.hint: Try the sentence with just the pronoun: Me built the volcano? or I built the volcano?
items.why: The doers of the action (subjects) use I, not me. It's also polite to name the other person first: Jordan and I.

items.wrong: The coach gave the trophy to Ana and I.
accept: The coach gave the trophy to Ana and me.
items.hint: Take Ana out: gave the trophy to I? or to me?
items.why: After a word like to, use the object pronoun: to me, not to I.

items.wrong: Liam made the cake hisself.
accept: Liam made the cake himself.
items.hint: Hisself isn't a word. What's the -self word for he?
items.why: The intensive pronoun for he is himself (hisself is not standard English).

items.wrong: When a student studies, they should take breaks.
accept: When students study, they should take breaks.
When a student studies, he or she should take breaks.
items.hint: A student is one person; they is usually used for more than one here. Make them match.
items.why: In school writing, make a pronoun match the number of the noun it stands for: students … they, or a student … he or she.

items.wrong: When Mia talked to Grace, she was upset.
accept: When Mia talked to Grace, Mia was upset.
When Mia talked to Grace, Grace was upset.
Mia was upset when she talked to Grace.
Grace was upset when Mia talked to her.
items.hint: Who was upset, Mia or Grace? Say the name instead of she.
items.why: A pronoun is vague when it could mean more than one person. Use the name to make it clear.

items.wrong: The list of chores are on the fridge.
accept: The list of chores is on the fridge.
items.hint: What is on the fridge: the list or the chores? Is that one thing or many?
items.why: The subject is list (one thing), so the verb is is. Of chores just describes the list.

items.wrong: Each of the students have a locker.
accept: Each of the students has a locker.
items.hint: Each means one at a time. One has or one have?
items.why: Each is singular, so it takes has.

items.wrong: Because the bus was late.
accept: We were late because the bus was late.
I was late because the bus was late.
Because the bus was late, we were late.
Because the bus was late, I was late.
Because the bus was late, we missed the start of school.
Because the bus was late, I missed the start of school.
items.hint: Because … what happened? Add what happened as a result.
items.why: A sentence starting with because needs a second part that says what happened. On its own it's a fragment.

items.wrong: I finished my book I started a new one.
accept: I finished my book. I started a new one.
I finished my book, and I started a new one.
I finished my book; I started a new one.
I finished my book, so I started a new one.
After I finished my book, I started a new one.
items.hint: There are two complete thoughts. Split them with a period, or join them with a comma and and.
items.why: Two complete sentences can't just run together. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word (and, so, but).

items.wrong: It was raining, we stayed inside.
accept: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
It was raining. We stayed inside.
It was raining; we stayed inside.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
We stayed inside because it was raining.
items.hint: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences. Add so, or use a period.
items.why: A comma by itself can't join two complete sentences (a comma splice). Add a joining word like so, or use a period or semicolon.

items.prompt: Move the describing part so it describes the right thing.
items.wrong: I saw a dog walking to school.
accept: Walking to school, I saw a dog.
While walking to school, I saw a dog.
While I was walking to school, I saw a dog.
I saw a dog while I was walking to school.
I saw a dog while walking to school.
items.hint: Who was walking to school, you or the dog? Put walking to school next to the right one.
items.why: Put a describing phrase next to the thing it describes; otherwise it sounds like the dog was walking to school.

items.wrong: It was a long boring movie.
accept: It was a long, boring movie.
items.hint: Could you say long and boring movie? If and works between two describing words, put a comma there.
items.why: When two adjectives describe a noun equally (you could put and between them), separate them with a comma.

items.wrong: The team won they're first game.
accept: The team won their first game.
items.hint: They're means they are. Does they are first game make sense?
items.why: Their shows belonging (their game). They're means they are. There is a place.

items.wrong: The dog wagged it's tail.
accept: The dog wagged its tail.
items.hint: It's means it is. Does wagged it is tail make sense?
items.why: Its shows belonging (its tail). It's always means it is or it has.

items.prompt: Add quotation marks and a comma.
items.wrong: Coach Diaz shouted Keep your eyes on the ball!
accept: Coach Diaz shouted, "Keep your eyes on the ball!"
items.hint: Who is talking, and what are their exact words? A comma goes after shouted.
items.why: A direct quotation gets quotation marks around the exact words, a comma before it, and a capital first word. The ! goes inside the closing mark.

items.prompt: Add quotation marks and a comma.
items.wrong: That was the best field trip ever said Priya.
accept: "That was the best field trip ever," said Priya.
items.hint: The quote comes first this time. What goes at the end of the quoted words instead of a period?
items.why: When the speaker comes after the quote, end the quoted words with a comma inside the closing mark: "…ever," said Priya.

items.wrong: Are we there yet? asked my little brother.
accept: "Are we there yet?" asked my little brother.
items.hint: A question mark already ends the quote. Does it go inside or outside the quotation mark?
items.why: A ? or ! that belongs to the quote goes inside the closing quotation mark, and then no comma is needed.

items.wrong: Mom said, "dinner is ready".
accept: Mom said, "Dinner is ready."
items.hint: Two things: the first word of a quote, and where the period goes.
items.why: Capitalize the first word of a quotation, and put the period inside the closing quotation mark.

items.wrong: When the rain stops said Dad we can go to the park.
accept: "When the rain stops," said Dad, "we can go to the park."
items.hint: The quote is split by said Dad. Each part gets its own quotation marks.
items.why: In a split quotation, close the first part with a comma inside the quote, put a comma after the speaker, and start the second part lowercase when it continues the same sentence.

items.wrong: "I finished my book," said Lena, "And now I want the next one."
accept: "I finished my book," said Lena, "and now I want the next one."
items.hint: Is the second part a new sentence, or the same sentence continuing?
items.why: When a split quotation is one sentence, the second part starts with a lowercase letter.

items.prompt: The text says: "Owls can turn their heads almost all the way around." Fix the quote so it uses the author's exact words.
items.wrong: The author says owls "can spin their heads all the way around."
accept: The author says owls "can turn their heads almost all the way around."
items.hint: Put the article sentence next to yours. Every word inside the quotation marks has to match.
items.why: Words inside quotation marks must be copied exactly from the text. If you change words, it is not a quotation anymore: copy it exactly, or leave out the quotation marks.

items.prompt: Fix the punctuation. Use either a comma OR that, not both.
items.wrong: The guide wrote that, "The trail is closed in winter."
accept: The guide wrote that "the trail is closed in winter."
The guide wrote, "The trail is closed in winter."
items.hint: With a comma you capitalize the quote. With that you use no comma and no capital.
items.why: Introduce a text quotation with a comma and a capital letter (wrote, "The…") or with that and no comma or capital (wrote that "the…"). Not both.

items.prompt: The text says: "Bees visit thousands of flowers every day." Add the quotation marks and punctuation.
items.wrong: The article explains that bees visit thousands of flowers every day
accept: The article explains that "bees visit thousands of flowers every day."
items.hint: Which words come straight from the text? They go inside quotation marks, and the period goes inside too.
items.why: Put the author's exact words in quotation marks. After that, the quote starts lowercase, and the period goes inside the closing mark.

items.wrong: Wow that cougar can jump really far.
accept: Wow! That cougar can jump really far.
Wow, that cougar can jump really far.
items.hint: Wow shows surprise. It needs an exclamation point or a comma after it.
items.why: An interjection is followed by an exclamation point (strong feeling, then a new sentence) or a comma (milder, same sentence).

items.prompt: Punctuate the dialogue and its interjection.
items.wrong: Oops I dropped the whole tray said Marco.
accept: "Oops! I dropped the whole tray," said Marco.
items.hint: Two jobs: punctuate Oops, and put the spoken words in quotation marks with a comma before said.
items.why: Oops shows surprise or embarrassment, so it takes an !. The spoken words go in quotation marks, ending with a comma before said Marco.

items.wrong: Hey wait for me!
accept: Hey, wait for me!
Hey! Wait for me!
items.hint: Hey is calling for attention. What comes right after it?
items.why: After an interjection like Hey, use a comma (same sentence) or an exclamation point (its own sentence, then capitalize the next word).
